Most areas had a framerate of 35-50, which is very disappointing for a high budget game. [h1]Overview[/h1]
[b]Quantum Break[/b] (QB) is a third person action game with heavy emphasis on storytelling. Players impersonate Jack Joyce, who recently came back to Riverport city after being called by his old friend Paul Serene, hearing how the latter is on the verge of an amazing scientific breakthrough. Things of course don't go as planned, and a major space-time distortion happens as consequence of this experiment. Both Jack and Paul are fully irradiated by the machine, and acquire phenomenal but dangerous time control powers. Each of them will try to use these skills for their own agendas, ultimately trying to prevent the End of Time caused by the experiment's failure. 

🟩 [b]Pros[/b]
[list]
[*]Extraordinary visual quality paired with very good art direction from start to end.
[*]Rather unique and enjoyable combat system focusing on time manipulation.
[*]An entire live action mini-series included between chapters, influenced by player choices.
[*]Good pacing that alternates action and story-focused sections quite well.
[*]Plenty of collectible lore items and upgrade points scattered in each level. 
[/list]
🟥 [b]Cons[/b]
[list]
[*]Severe optimization problems make this title extremely demanding.
[*]Poor variety of enemy types, weapons to use.
[*]Character movement is clunky with Mouse + Keyboard.
[*]The final boss fight is disappointing and anticlimactic.
[/list]

Starting with the good points, it's safe to say one of the most impressive features of Quantum Break resides in its visuals, which can stand up among the best even today, despite this title being from 2016. Not only models, effects, animations and environments are all of top quality, but also there is an evident care in crafting each environment to perfection and minute detail. The combat is as well one of its strong suits, delivering a unique system based on conventional shooting paired with time manipulation, and an emphasis on environment use to overcome enemy forces.

Putting an entire TV-like series filmed with real actors in-between chapters is something I've not seen in any other game to date. Not only that, but it also changes based on story choices. QB alternates shooting phases with sizable exploration focused segments, without any of the two things being dominant - this results in very good pacing. Especially in these latter sections, there are plenty of upgrade points and lore items to collect to know more about the story.

For the bad side of things the worst problem is clearly optimization, making the game consume an ungodly amount of processing power across the board. Partially this is justified by the visuals sure, but it does go past even that. Enemies and weapons on paper are varied but they all feel too similar between each other, and are often copies of weaker ones just with better rate of fire, damage or HP in the case of foes. 

[b]Overall, Quantum Break remains a very good experience that delivers a rather unique setting, original take on combat and well done story, characters. The problems are definitely overcome by the good points and this game will be enjoyed by 3rd person action fans that want to try something unusual. It took me around 13 hours to finish the game on Hard, while also watching all live-action episodes and reading most lore material. There is some replay value thanks to the choice system but not much. For the regular price of 37€, I would suggest waiting for a sale before buying.[/b]

[h1]In-Depth Breakdown[/h1]
🎮 [b]Gameplay Analysis[/b]
Gameplay is divided into Exploration, Puzzles, Upgrading and Combat.

[b]Exploration[/b]
Is performed on foot, traversing various environments ranging from abandoned warehouses to high-security underground bunkers. One of Jack's powers, Time Vision, will allow him to see any item of interest within a large radius while standing still - that includes lore documents, upgrade points, echoes of past events, enemies and explosive materials. This makes finding things a lot easier. 

There are plenty of documents to read to know more about the story, setting and characters - some of these interactions count as Ripples, which can change the course of story in a modest way. Many transitions are one-way drops in otherwise semi-open environments, so make sure you get everything before proceeding, backtracking is rarely possible. 

[b]Puzzles[/b]
Are generally linked to using time manipulation to traverse otherwise impassable locations. They vary from collapsing a cargo container, getting on it, then rewinding time to lift it up again, to using time dilation to avoid automated defenses. They are never overly difficult to overcome. 

[b]Upgrading[/b]
Is performed in a special menu at any time, provided you have enough points, gained from finding Chronon Sources, very bright spheres only visible by using Time Vision. Upgrades will always cost 2, 4 and 6 points, often increasing duration, range or effectiveness of Jack's skills. They can really make a big difference during the most difficult fights.

[b]Combat[/b]
Plays out like a traditional third-person shooter, using a shoulder focused aiming reticle and a cover-based system, automatically used when approaching any solid object large enough. However both Jack and more advanced enemies possess some for of time manipulation abilities, which range from freezing foes in place for a few seconds, freezing bullets mid air with a shield, or using a localized time distortion as a bomb. Most enemies will be susceptible to these powers, but advanced ones will often require outmaneuvering them to hit a specific weak spot. 

Environments have a high grade of destructibility, most structures will be torn to pieces by bullets and explosions, while shooting explosive canisters or Chronon barrels will unleash respectively explosions or time anomalies. Generally on Hard enemies hit quite hard and a few shots will be enough to take you down - using your powers to strike quickly then go back to cover will be the best approach. In case of death, you will restart from the last checkpoint.

Quantum Break follows the consequences of a time travel experiment to which Paul Serene invites his old friend Jack Joyce.. with all the drastic results such things normally have. The story is thrilling enough, especially if you like the time travel genre. Quantum Break also implements time altering abilities of the protagonist in the gameplay - both for the riddles/jump´n run part as well as the action part.

Where QB also does an interesting mix is the presentation of the story/game itself. The ingame characters are made after real life actors, with which the normal game episodes are also mixed through, after every ingame episode one part of a four part movie series advances the storyline. Complementing that fact is that nearly all actors are experienced from other series and enrich the game in their roles.

Add to all this points quite some humor in the many texts you can find in the game (there is enough to look out for, for achievement hunters as well as hidden object hunters) as well as a bit emotion in the right places...

So in the end the only downsides i could find are maybe a bit of an open ending and a really annoying boss fight. 

Conclusio: I enjoyed the series as well as the game and liked the presentation of the game very much. Through the "time rifts" the graphics more often than not seem a bit strange, but that´s ok. I really liked how they implemented the manipulation of time into the riddles and the presentation of real life actors in the gameplay graphics.
In the end i didn´t expect too much from Quantum Break at the beginning, but it quickly became one of my games of the year 2016.

I saw this game as a teen back in 2016 and thought "WOW, Quantum Break (QB) is going to be the shit!" Finally picked it up on a Steam sale within the last few years and wanted to try it out. After completing the game 100%, I can confidently say that the game was an overall mediocre experience. 

This is one of those times Steam really needs a middle ground option since this game is just... okay all around. I will say I felt disappointed with QB as it provides an interesting perspective on manipulating time, which while cool, felt as if there was so much more they could have done with it. Besides that, this game is plagued by really average gun play crammed into it. Certain battles become a chore to complete rather than really wanting to progress the game. This is especially true in a few of the "boss" battles that are made harder by the game's gun play.

The story on the other hand is actually pretty alright. Nothing really outstanding in any department, but I did enjoy it overall. The biggest problem with this game from a story perspective is that its pacing is bizarre. After you complete an Act (of which there are five total) you are greeted with a full-length live action show that pieces together stuff happening off screen that's still good to know. However I found that these were just really boring and stopped me from actually playing the game. I ended up just skipping these and had a much more cohesive experience. 

In conclusion, this game feels like a 2016 game. The graphics, the game play (including the worst checkpoints I've ever seen in any video game), and the story all feel pretty dated. If you buy this, you'll end up playing it through one time and will never touch it again. Nothing wrong with that, but there are better games to spend your money on. Also, to touch on the graphics a bit more, the highest the game naively goes to is 1080p. On your PC, go to %AppData% -> Local -> QuantumBreak and open up the "renderer" file with notepad. You can change your aspect ratio to something higher. I played it through changing it to 1440p with any issues. Hope this review was able to help someone, and if you've read this far, thank you! If you decide to take the plunge, I wish you all the best in your time travel adventures!

[b]Quantum Break[/b] stands as a curious relic of its time. 

It's impressive to note that the game was conceived and developed four years before Christopher Nolan's [i]Tenet[/i], yet it carries a similarly stylized sci-fi action approach, experimenting with time and transforming it into a weapon. Two years before [i]Detroit: Become Human[/i], Remedy was already showcasing photorealistic graphics and animations. Even eight years later, the game holds up reasonably well—its emotions and facial expressions in cutscenes are meant to blend seamlessly with live-action segments, pushing the game toward the realm of a high-budget TV series. However, the 720p resolution, a vestige of last-generation consoles, is noticeable.

The level design is distinctly familiar, echoing past Remedy titles like [i]Alan Wake[/i]. It feels crude and straightforward, reminiscent of an early 2000s era when [i]Max Payne[/i] was on everyone's lips. You might find yourself stuck at times, unsure of what to do next, but "quantum sense" hints will guide you in the right direction. Surprisingly, the enemy AI is competent—they’re fast, agile; the shooting mechanics, however, are simplistic. There's no stealth; you either move, dash, or automatically take cover behind walls or boxes. The superpowers, though functional, often lack impact. The transitions between abilities are clunky, which can be frustrating.

Sam Lake aimed to blur the line between cinema and video games. While [b]Quantum Break[/b] can be likened to projects from [i]Quantic Dream[/i] or Hideo Kojima, it falls short of delivering engaging gameplay and deeper narrative exposition. It avoids becoming a pure cinematic experience but never reaches the fluidity of controlling Norman Reedus in [i]Death Stranding[/i]. The protagonist here feels stiff, like an outdated puppet with no upgrade system. The game is linear, offering little replay value despite its branching storylines. There’s no consistent rhythm: at times, you’re nudged to discover notes and read letters, but then you’re hurried to press forward.

Yet, some of the "time-reversal" moments are genuinely impressive—be it a shipwreck or a bridge explosion. These are well-crafted set pieces.

[b]Quantum Break[/b] desperately wants to be a masterpiece, and for its ambition alone, much can be forgiven. Unfortunately, underdeveloped gameplay mechanics make it a one-time playthrough. 

Still, despite many rough edges and far from ideal moments, it’s really worth playing, especially when on sale. [b]Quantum Break[/b] has a soul and an auteur's touch—something most games sorely lack. You can feel the love that went into creating it, and that means a lot.

Rating: 8/10
Genre: Third Person Shooter 

The Good:
+ The time related visual effects are impressive both in gameplay and in cinematic moments. Killing enemies causes them to remain frozen in time, visual discrepancies and distorted effects are used in great effect to show how the world is changing.  

+ The UI is exceptionally well done. Every chapter/section has its own UI screen detailing story elements, the amount and type of collectable in each section and a timeline where the collectable is approximately located in the chapter. All relevant information is laid out in a clean and easy to use format. 

+ The game is very story driven, and everything is executed well. The characters are believable, each one has its own motivations, the dialogue is well written in addition to great voice acting. In typical fashion, a lot of back story is told through audiologs, emails, documents that you find in each chapter.  This is a story about time travel so obviously if you think to hard about it you will find plot loopholes. I find its best to just accept things with these types of stories just to enjoy it. To Remedy’s credit they spent a great deal of time on the story and mapping everything out so that there is some consistency involved. 

+ Gameplay is a typical third person shooter mixed with special powers.  You automatically take cover when you get near a wall/barrier without the need of pressing a button, which helps keep things moving along smoothly. Most of the powers help you gain an advantage in battle with all of them having a cooldown effect so you can’t over abuse them. They all have some uses although I did find the time dodge power to be the most useful. The only downside is that the shooting sections of the game don’t change too much throughout the entirety of the game. You entire an area, kill all the enemies and then move on. 
 

The Average:
+/- After every act you are treated to a live action “movie” to further the story. These movies are well shot, look nice and have some variations depending on the choices you make during gameplay but also feel out of place in a videogame. They reminded me of the live action full motion videos in the 90’s when it was starting to become a fad in pc gaming. These movies are 20- 30 minutes in length and just breakup the entire pace of the game. It feels like a huge waste of resources that could have gone directly into adding more to the game.  


The Bad:
- I played on the hardest difficulty so this may not apply to the lower difficulties. The hard difficulty is actually pretty easy compared to other games. There were a few frustrating sections, a sniper can kill you in 2 shots but for the most part, playing smart and making good use of your powers will allow you to get passed anything in your way. The last boss battle however is when good game design is thrown out the window. I don’t want to spoil anything so I will just say the last boss battle can be very frustrating, not because its hard per se, but because of some poor design decision. I died more times in this battle then almost the entire game.  

Conclusion: 
A fun, well executed game that deals with time travel.

I have often wondered how hard it could be to create a world and style that is believable but at the same time majestic for games taking place in alternative realities. Wolfenstein: The New Order was one of the few games that got this right, creating massive and interesting architecture supported by a coherent, distinct style while still remaining within the confines of real world physics. Considering that the world design in its sequel, The New Colossus was not built in the same vein, the answer seems to be “pretty hard”.

There are very few games that achieve this and Quantum Break is one of them. Within five minutes of starting a new game, you’ll see two contrasting buildings, a modern Physics building and the more classical library. Both of them are designed within the realm of believability but on the other hand, they have some minor touches that establish this perception of being in an alternative reality. As the game progresses, indoor spaces will have more futuristic look with a certain sense of extravagance and this will keep being contrasted by the rundown look of the places that are used by the game’s protagonists, establishing a clear sense of divide between “the good” and “the bad”.

Finding even this type of environmental storytelling with unique visuals would allow most games to set themselves apart from the usual rabble. For Quantum Break, this is just the beginning. As an example, one of the most striking accomplishments of the game is the use of particle effects. Particle effects have been in games for such a long time but to see them being used as a major part of how the world and its events are conveyed to the player is a testament to how a nonconforming, unified, imaginative art direction can elevate a game.

Quantum Break shattered and went beyond all my expectations with its world and did the same thing again with its story. Gaming in general, unfortunately, is not on the same level of traditional media when it comes to writing but this is another facet where Quantum Break is simply exceptional. The logic behind time travel and its consistencies holds up throughout the game with interesting characters that have solid motives and backgrounds without being too overt about their intentions. Expository dialogue never turns into a lecture and the flow of conversations are natural and informative. Impeccable facial animations and all around great level of acting especially helped with initial engagement to the story and it has been a delight watching Aidan Gillen and Lance Reddick together after The Wire, in a similar hierarchy as well.

Like a great TV series Quantum Break always had me impatiently moving to the next chapter with so many details only noticeable if you pay attention to the background and the variety of video recordings, emails. Even reading random notes, dossiers etc. located inside the offices that does not show an interaction prompt have so many details to them. If you want to enjoy Quantum Break fully, I recommend reading every piece of information thoroughly and focusing on every scene even though skimming is usually fine in most games.

The live action TV series in between however, does not benefit from same strengths. It mostly focuses on side characters and tosses amazing time stutter/manipulation effects out of the window. It does not have that amazing direction and consistency found within the game. Northlight, Remedy’s narrative engine, does better visuals than 720p streaming with film grain anyway. Brief focuses on other characters is a good idea for this game and instead of live action making them shorter gameplay segments with a few gameplay mechanics unique to characters thrown in would have benefited the game a lot more. 

When Max Payne first came out it gave us a much simpler experience of time manipulation mechanics called bullet time but even that was an amazing experience for a generation that just had been stunned by The Matrix two years before Max Payne. The ongoing impact of The Matrix for my generation cannot be overstated. So many cousins were kicked in the chest right after “I know kung-fu” yell and so many walls had foot prints after failed wall running attempts. Although Jack Joyce is not as capable in hand to hand combat, you can only time rush and tackle a single enemy, his six different time manipulation skills is as close to being Neo in a game. Especially time dodge and time spot will come in handy in combat but each skill has different uses and basic puzzle platforming parts where you employ these skills provide a good change of pace. I wish there were more of these sequences and the difficulty was a bit more “puzzling”, nevertheless seeing that time skills are not only useful for combat leads you to think more about the true extent of time manipulation.

For all its various enemy types, weapons and different skills, action parts of Quantum Break fail to take advantage of its strengths. Mouse feels like moving an analogue stick and does not allow twitchy movement. Controlling Jack is not a smooth experience and he takes too long to respond to direction changes, he may even sometimes get stuck in place. As your time skills evolve these can be easier to ignore as you would be feeling like a god, albeit a clunky one, if you can get past the opening moments that are not quite enjoyable.

I had also praised graphics before and they truly hold up even today (this game had the most detailed rug patterns I have ever seen, my mind was truly blown) but I also did quit the game five minutes in, to look for a fix for the terrible motion blur. All the details Remedy has built in the game are just a random blur if you play this vanilla and I am not exaggerating. Probably, a lot of compromises were made to make this game playable on an Xbox One. Thankfully, there is the Helix Mod that completely removes the blur with other added enhancements. Don’t forget to turn off upscaling from settings as well. I don’t think I could have played this game that I enjoyed immensely without the Helix Mod (sadly, Steam overlay does not work with Helix Mod, meaning that I could not take screenshots in one of the most screenshottable games ever made).

The term cinematic experience has been thrown around so many times for console games with a mediocre story and lacking engaging gameplay that it lost all meaning. Quantum Break on the other hand is “the” cinematic experience without all the caveats and baggage the term brings. If action was smoother, live action sequences were gameplay and Helix Mod was incorporated into the game this could have been a masterpiece. Nevertheless, it became one of the games that I wish I could erase from my mind and experience again.

Overall, this game is okay, but there are a lot of issues.

[h2] Technical and Optimization [/h2]

For a game that came out almost a decade ago now, visually the game looks amazing, like it could've been released within the past 2-3 years. This was the first time Remedy was using their proprietary engine, Northlight, on a project, and you can tell. The game is VERY unoptimized, but it sorta makes sense with all the tech Remedy crammed in here. For one, this game has a very early version of what now every game includes: upscaling. I think this has to be one of the first games to include some form of upscaling, and I respect Remedy for using new tech and being ahead of its time, but obviously during 2016 the tech was not as advanced or optimized as it is now, leading to this game having a setting where you can lock the game to 30fps. I played on a 3070Ti at medium-high settings, and the game kept fluctuating between 120fps and 60fps with constant frame drops to the point where I just locked it at 60fps. On most parts of the game, I was able to maintain a steady 60fps but, there are some levels that are super unoptimized, like the bridge one. I can only imagine what the performance was on early GTX cards...

[h2] Combat [/h2]

The game has decent combat, gunplay is serviceable, and the time abilities are fun with new ones getting added as the story progresses so you don't get bored. I will admit though, combat did get pretty repetitive and stale near the end of the game, but it's fine. For an early Remedy game that was released after Alan Wake, they were clearly trying to do something new with combat, and they definitely improved on this aspect compared to their past games.

[h2] Story [/h2]

It's Remedy. You are probably playing this game for its story in the first place, and like all of Remedy's other games, it's good. Is it better than Alan Wake or Max Payne? No. But is it terrible? Also no. There are a lot of cool elements in this game, and I enjoyed most of the characters. Jack is a decent protagonist, not too memorable but has some good moments. Paul is a decent antagonist with okay motivations and a couple of standout scenes near the later parts of the game. Beth is one of the better characters with an interesting storyline. William is also pretty good, even if he is barely in the game. I would say the one character I liked the most was definitely Lance Reddick's character (Rest in Peace). He steals the show here with many great moments and [spoiler] the clues of him being chronon enabled/being a shifter are nicely done, and I wished they explored more on this idea of a being that can exist in many different dimensions at once (I guess Remedy did do this 7 years later in Alan Wake 2 with Mr. Door, which is just Mr. Hatch but reworked because Remedy didn't get the rights to Quantum Break and sadly Lance passed away) [/spoiler]. I love time travel stories, so I was hoping this game would focus more on that, but the stuff they did focus on with the chronon and closed loops are cool concepts that I enjoyed. The rest of the story... it's fine, it's got some decent time stuff mixed in with okay to great characters and some good writing here and there. I did like the ending and it makes sense that Jack is becoming similar to Paul (in the sense of his powers and sickness), but it all kind of feels pointless since it's just a setup to a sequel that never happened. I probably would've liked the sequel to this game more since it seemed like it was going to focus on Mr. Hatch.

[h2] The Gimmick [/h2]

This game's gimmick is that it's a game but also a TV show, which is kind of cool because Remedy has been doing live-action stuff for their games since Max Payne, and it's clear they have a love for it. Is it executed perfectly in this game? No. But it does help expand the story and some minor characters in ways that would've been boring if they had just been gameplay segments. Also, your choices in the game affecting the episodes is a nice touch and does fit well with the game.

[h2] Final Thoughts [/h2]

The game kind of just feels like sequel bait, but to be honest, all of Remedy's games sort of are. I really like what Remedy is doing with the whole Remedy Connected Universe, but at the same time, it also means that literally every single one of their games is just sequel bait, and you just have to wait to see if that specific franchise gets a sequel or if another Remedy game comes out that is in some someway connected or builds upon the previous (You can tell Control builds upon Quantum Break for example). The ending for Quantum Break is 100% setting up a Quantum Break 2, but Remedy didn't get the rights to make a sequel, and they moved on to Control, which was honestly for the best. Overall, the game is okay. It has its moments but it's definitely one of Remedy's weakest games.

One does not play Quantum Break. This becomes quite evident in the game's vocabulary, preferring to refer to itself as a "show" rather than a "game". The game's format is novel in both senses of the word. Five "acts" separated by four 20 minute live-action episodes showing what happened as a result of the previous choices you made. Those episodes, along with interminable follow-the-character-through-the-environment-whilst-they-explain-the-story-to-you sequences, interspersed with brief moments of mildly inventive third-person shooter combat means that you do not actually play this game, you watch it. You watch it, as the passive spectator you are.

Let's cover... combat! The only noticable part of the game that can actually be considered gameplay involves shootouts featuring conveniently placed chest-high cover and your collection of six "time bending" super-powers. Four of those superpowers are limited to simply slowing or stopping time while another two of those superpowers have no discernable effect on time at all. Despite having six of these, you will only regularly use the four which require a single button push, and forget about the other two completely because those other two would actually require you to aim. You will solely reserve aiming for shooting people with your guns.

The high point of this game is the graphics. Very pretty. That's where your 70 GB went. The graphical niceties include the 3D scanned likenesses of the real cast members. I'm fairly sure Lance Riddick's own model is accurate down to the pimple's on the back of his neck (which are unreasonably close to the camera at one point which is how I know this...). This reinforces the point that the point of the game is to be looked at, rather than played. In the game, you are required to go to various points to hold a button next to a glowing light in order to upgrade your superpowers. I'm fairly sure this mechanic exists just to get you to look at the marvellous scenery. One thing I'd like to know is if those live-action episodes, are streamed from your hard drive or the internet. For 70 GB, it had better be the former.

On the topic of choices, the game has four main "junctions" where you choose between two conflicting major outcomes of the junction decision. The choice you make will alter the course of history itself and lead the game to eventually conclude with wildly different endings... which are all completely identical. That is to say that no decision I made had any impact whatsoever on what happened to the protagonist at any given point. I still ended up doing the exact same things in the same order to reach the same conclusion. The only notable difference is which characters perform any given action. One character seems to exist solely to fill the shoes of the person who would have been there, had they not died moments earlier due to a decision you made. Having played the game twice to encompass all possible choices, I can see no way in which the game is distinguishable from one that is entirely linear. This game[b] is [/b]linear; the decisions merely decide whether the paint on the walls is white or snow coloured.

You can watch this show if you want, I'll be getting 70 GB worth of hard drive back.

As videogames about time travel go, Quantum Break holds up incredibly well, boasting a foolproof narrative structure that never contradicts itself (not even once, I dare say — a particularly rare feat considering the premise’s infamous volatility as a storytelling device). It definitely ranks among the most coherent, tightly constructed stories based on the premise that I’ve had the pleasure of enjoying in any medium ever.

If anything, it only goes to show that the time travel conceit serves as a formidable fiction-writing challenge, where creative minds are made to hone and put their sense of storytelling economy into practice (or, in this case, words). The best time travel stories that are founded on consistently sound internal logic have no room for superfluous gestures and throwaway tics; everything has to serve a purpose — if not in the current scene, then most certainly later.

Yet there’s more to time travel stories than their paradoxical, often rigid mechanics, as there’s certainly more to stories in general beyond mere grammar. Quantum Break is great not because of its strict adherence to its own established logic (although it definitely helps), but rather because it’s ultimately a story about letting go and moving forward — the past cannot be altered, but the future still can.

Quantum Break is a good game, although the weakest shooter from Remedy. The time-travelling story is intriguing with good characters and occasional wobbly dialogue. The story choices don’t change enough to encourage a replay. Sadly, the ending is unsatisfying, leaving itself wide open for a sequel.

Gameplay wise, the shooting is enjoyable; you use various time powers to dash, slow, and create frozen time bubbles. But there isn’t enough of it in the 10 hour game. Several hours are taken up by the TV show interludes that mesh well with the game. There is basically one long combat sequence every few hours and a bunch near the end. The rest of the game is threadbare with shooting, choosing instead to mix in weak platforming and bland time puzzles between a handful of enemies. 

Visually it has some great time effects and characters look nice in cut scenes, but otherwise it’s not worth the mediocre performance. Upscaling was required just to ensure the camera didn’t jitter when running around, and even then it wasn’t smooth enough for pleasant shooting.

If you liked Remedy’s previous games then you will probably enjoy Quantum Break, but it’s not as strong as Alan Wake or Max Payne. Good pickup for around $10-20.

Really enjoyed Quantum Break! The live-action episodes were a nice break from gameplay, the combat and time powers were a blast, and the story had me hooked enough to finish it in just 2 days!

The game is part video game, part live action TV show, which is a really unique experience in itself. Actions in the game (as well as discoveries) will influence what you see in both the story and the TV show. It could be considered rather risky using both of these formats for in conjunction, but Remedy pulls it off beautifully. The show is action packed and well acted, while the game itself is so stunning to look at that at certain points, through little lighting nuances, it is impossible to distinguish between the real actors and their digital counterparts. The story is equally compelling; Time is ending and it is up to Jack Joyce (Shawn Ashmore in a compelling and brilliantly performed role) and his few allies to save the universe. Despite dealing with time travel and advanced quantum physics, the story is not too complex to follow. Jack Joyce makes it quite clear that he is no quantum physicist, much like the majority of people playing the game, and the story takes this into account. There are plenty of twists and little moments where you remember something from earlier in the story that seemed irrelevant at the time, but nothing too strenuous to follow. Gameplay wise, it is well crafted. Joyce moves with ease, his developing "time" powers are easily accessible, simple to upgrade and suitably potent in their effects (without being "godslayer" powerful) which is precisely what one would expect from manipulation of time itself. The visual effects throughout the game regarding Jack's powers and time itself are equally mesmerising and well animated. Gun play and combat is also suitably frantic, with intelligent enemies who will use team tactics (such as suppress and flank) to take you down. My only minor qualm with gun play is the camera. It's fine most of the time and easy to aim, but it has an awful habit of swapping shoulders after taking cover. It's easily fixed with a click of the stick so it is negligible in the grand scheme. I would also like to note that collectibles and intel' items are relatively easy to locate, which is fine, but reaching them can sometimes be a puzzle, which is also fine in terms of providing a challenge. I highly recommend it to anyone and everyone. 8.5 out of 10, nice work Remedy!

Quantum Break — Time, Tragedy and the Elegance of a Sci-Fi Masterpiece

There are games that entertain you.
There are games that impress you technically.
There are games that deliver a good story and then quietly disappear from memory.

And then there is Quantum Break — a game that, for me, belongs in that rare category of single-player experiences that do not simply occupy your time, but leave an emotional and intellectual imprint long after you stop playing.

This is not just a third-person action game with time powers.
This is not just a sci-fi shooter.
This is not just another experiment in cinematic storytelling.

Quantum Break is a bold, elegant and emotionally charged fusion of science fiction, tragedy, action, live-action drama, temporal philosophy and human consequence. It is one of those games that dared to be different, dared to be ambitious and dared to tell a story about time not only as a gameplay mechanic, but as a curse, a weapon, a prison and a tragedy.

For me, Quantum Break stands beside games like Mafia I, Mafia II, Uncharted, Sleeping Dogs and Cyberpunk 2077 in that special emotional territory where the game becomes more than entertainment. These are games that create atmosphere. Games that create memory. Games that make you feel something. Games that remind you that single-player storytelling is still one of the most powerful forms of gaming when it is executed with intelligence, confidence and artistic vision.

And Quantum Break absolutely belongs there.

From the very beginning, the game has a unique identity. It does not feel generic. It does not feel manufactured by committee. It has that unmistakable Remedy personality: cinematic, strange, atmospheric, mysterious, emotional and slightly surreal. It understands that a good science-fiction story is not only about technology, laboratories, timelines and paradoxes. It is about people trapped inside consequences they barely understand.

That is what makes Quantum Break so strong.

At the center of the story is Jack Joyce, a man thrown into an impossible situation after an experiment goes catastrophically wrong. What begins as a scientific breakthrough becomes a temporal disaster. Time itself fractures, reality becomes unstable, and Jack is forced into a conflict where the enemy is not only a corporation, not only an army, not only one man’s ambition — but the collapse of time.

That concept alone is powerful.

But what makes it work is that Quantum Break never treats time travel as a cheap gimmick. It treats it as something dangerous, tragic and almost spiritual. Time is not a toy here. It is not a simple excuse for cool powers. It is a force that breaks lives, destroys certainty, twists loyalty and turns every choice into a possible catastrophe.

That is excellent science fiction.

The best sci-fi does not simply ask, “What if technology became advanced?”
It asks, “What happens to humanity when technology reaches a place we are emotionally unprepared to control?”

Quantum Break understands that question perfectly.

The story is built around consequence. Around cause and effect. Around the terrifying idea that the future may already be wounded by the choices of the present. Around the possibility that trying to prevent disaster may actually become the path that creates it. That kind of narrative complexity gives the game a deeper intellectual weight than many action titles even attempt.

And yet, despite its complexity, the story remains emotionally accessible.

It is about friendship.
It is about betrayal.
It is about brotherhood.
It is about fear.
It is about power.
It is about people making desperate choices while reality collapses around them.

That emotional grounding is essential.

Because without human emotion, time travel stories become cold puzzles. Quantum Break avoids that. It gives the concept a heartbeat.

Jack Joyce is not interesting only because he gains powers. He is interesting because he is not prepared for the responsibility forced upon him. He is not a superhero. He is a man trying to understand a disaster while being hunted, manipulated and pushed into events that are already bigger than him. His time powers make him dangerous, but they do not make him invulnerable emotionally.

That is important.

The game constantly reminds you that power does not eliminate fear. Sometimes power simply gives you a better view of the disaster coming toward you.

Then there is Paul Serene, one of the most fascinating antagonists in modern gaming. He is not a simple villain. He is not evil in a childish way. He is dangerous because he believes he is right. He has seen things others have not seen. He understands the catastrophe from a perspective that makes his actions feel, in his own mind, necessary.

That is what makes him compelling.

A weak villain wants power for no reason.
A strong villain believes his brutality is rational.

Paul Serene is terrifying because he is not chaotic. He is controlled. Calculated. Haunted. He is a man who has turned trauma into ideology. He believes he is saving the world, even if saving the world requires sacrificing people, morality and freedom.

That kind of antagonist elevates the entire story.

The dynamic between Jack and Paul gives Quantum Break its dramatic tension. They are not just hero and villain. They are connected by time, by science, by consequence and by different interpretations of survival. Jack represents resistance, emotion and moral urgency. Paul represents control, inevitability and cold pragmatism. Their conflict is not only physical. It is philosophical.

Can the future be changed?
Should it be changed?
What if preventing the end requires becoming monstrous?
What if accepting destiny is just another form of cowardice?

These questions give the game depth.

And that is one of the reasons I respect Quantum Break so much. It is an action game that actually has ideas.

The gameplay itself is extremely satisfying because the time powers are not cosmetic. They define the rhythm of combat. Quantum Break does not play like a standard cover shooter with one or two abilities added on top. It turns time manipulation into a core combat language.

You can freeze enemies.
You can dash through danger.
You can create temporal shields.
You can distort the battlefield.
You can turn movement itself into a weapon.

Combat becomes a dance of momentum, precision and temporal aggression. You are not simply hiding behind cover and exchanging bullets. You are bending the flow of battle. You are moving through time fractures, repositioning, disrupting enemies, controlling pressure and creating cinematic violence in real time.

That is brilliant.

The best moments in Quantum Break feel like playing through a high-budget sci-fi action sequence where you are both the director and the protagonist. Bullets hang in the air. Enemies are suspended in temporal distortion. Explosions freeze, shimmer and then erupt. Jack moves through chaos like reality itself is struggling to keep up with him.

That is not just gameplay.

That is style.

And Remedy has always understood style.

Graphically, Quantum Break is still an impressive game. It has a very specific visual identity: clean, cinematic, moody, modern, cold and dramatic. The lighting is excellent. The facial detail, environments, particle effects and time distortion visuals create a world that feels polished and atmospheric. It may not be the newest title anymore, but its art direction gives it longevity.

The time fracture effects are especially memorable. They are not just visual effects for spectacle. They communicate that reality is damaged. Objects stutter. Environments collapse and rebuild. Time becomes unstable, almost physical. You can see the world breaking.

That visual language is one of the game’s strongest achievements.

Quantum Break is unique mix of a time manipulation third person shooter game, and a live action show.

After a catastrophic event involving a time machine occurs, time has become fractured, giving two people the powers to manipulate time itself. You mainly play as the protagonist Jack Joyce, and you’re trying to fix time before it’s too late. You also play briefly as the antagonist Paul Serene, where you make four separate choices that directly change how the story is told.

I love using time manipulation abilities in games, and Quantum Break is no exception. I enjoyed the combat very much. It’s fun and fast paced, but the combat kind of easy, and it’s very forgiving because you start regenerating extremely quickly. The character movement feels responsive, but there is auto crouching when you go near cover, so it may take some people a little getting used to.

You will also need to use these powers outside of combat to progress through some of the areas. There are upgrades for your abilities that let you use them more often and more effectively.

[h1]Pros:[/h1]
[list][*]the story, and concept of how time works are interesting
[*]the script is written very well, and watching how the decisions played out as a live show with such a phenomenal cast is really enjoyable
[*]voice acting, music and the sound effects are done well
[*]cinematics looked absolutely amazing, and they really captured the actors likeness and expressions incredibly well
[*]combat is fun, fast paced, and forgiving - you can rush in and kill a bunch of enemies, and bail out to find cover if you start taking too much damage
[*]full controller and mouse and keyboard support
[*]making different decisions allows for some replay value (After finishing the game with my original set of choices, I went back and made different ones to see how the live show played out. Some parts of each episode were the same, but there were also several things that were changed, which in turn also affected the following chapters slightly.)
[*]upgrade points are easy to find without having to go too much out of your way, but there are lots of other collectibles to be found that give you more insight into the story for those who like to take the time and explore more thoroughly[/list]

[h1]Cons:[/h1]
[list][*]performance wise, the game is not optimized the greatest (on ultra settings, 40-60 frames using a GTX 970 with periodic frame drops into the 30s; lowered the settings to high and was getting about 50-60 frames consistently)
[*]there were some times during gameplay that the characters looked grainy (usually when lots of other stuff was happening at the same time) - it was noticeable, but certainly not game breaking
[*]mouse thumb buttons bind as "null," and even though they work properly, all the prompts in game say "null" as well
[*](nitpick) no way to tone down or turn off the motion blur
[*](nitpick) some of the load times were a slower than I would have liked (even using a SSD)
[*](nitpick) when trying to climb onto some objects, you have to re-position or come from a different angle to be able to climb up[/list]

[h1]Conclusion:[/h1]
The game took me about 9-9.5 hours or so, and I really enjoyed the gameplay as well as the show that’s incorporated into the overall experience. Although, I am already using Windows 10, I’m glad that they made the game compatible with Windows 7 and available on Steam. I wound up playing the whole game in one sitting. I really liked the game, and recommend it to those who like time manipulation games combined with a well-told story rich experience. Keep in mind though, the performance optimization needs some improvement, so even with the recommended GTX 970, don’t expect a solid 60 frames per second on ultra settings.

[h1][b]Two in One[/b][/h1]
[i]You (Jack Joyce) are invited to Riverport by your best friend Paul Serene. He needs help with an experiment at the University. Soon, you will find out that it is a time machine based on chronon particles, and Paul needs you to start it. Like in the first Half-life game, something will go wrong, and you will witness an incident that causes a time fracture. You and Paul are hit by a large amount of chronon particles that give both of you special abilities. Here comes your brother William, and your journey to save the world has just begun.[/i]

[h2]Time's Beginning[/h2]
The story is divided into five acts and four parts of a TV series. Yes, the game is not only a game, but it also has a live-action series, each episode is about 25 minutes long, and the same awesome actors are in both. The best is Lance Reddick as the mysterious Martin Hatch, who is Paul's right-hand man. The story has only one ending, but you can make some decisions that affect the future events in the next acts and episodes. Whatever path you choose, it will make sense because someone who wrote the story has taken his time and used his brain.

[h2]Game(time)play[/h2]
During your path to save the world, you will face guards from Monarch Solutions – Paul’s organization, from simple guys with a pistol to heavily armored soldiers with machine guns. You can use their weapons, but you also have some special abilities that you gain at the beginning. Your main skill is time vision which you can use to reveal enemies or return an object to state before present to clear your path. Also, you can stop time, quickly dash a few meters to the future, stop bullets like in Matrix and more. Thanks to this, fights are unique and fun to play. The game is a linear action-adventure, but there is space to explore each location, and you should do it because you can find many collectables and upgrade your skills by collecting Chronon sources. The story is not long (about 7-10 hours), so there is no need to rush. I played it twice because I wanted to find everything and see what other choices could change.

During my playthrough, I encountered some bugs as well. For some reason, after approximately two hours of playing, I got a weird blacked-out background a few meters in front of me, but restarting the game solved the issue. There seems to be a problem with the NVIDIA drivers, or perhaps something is wrong with the optimisation. Also, during one level, I fell into a void after entering a certain room. I thought it was a bug of doors that shouldn't open, but after playing the story a second time, I found out there was an actual room. The last problem was with a TV series. It’s built into the game, but it isn't stored locally, it only streams from the Internet. It would be nice if there was an option to download all the episodes because once I couldn't watch an episode. I just got a streaming error, so I had to watch it on YouTube.

[h2]Timeless Visual[/h2]
Otherwise, the game worked well, and it still looks nice nowadays, especially the time effects are superb. You will encounter many weird and funny events as well. When time temporarily stops, it’s caused by the fraction that you and Paul made, you can literally walk around flying bullets, see other NPC paused in certain positions and so on. It’s unique in games and it looks awesome. Along with a great soundtrack, the game offers a nice atmosphere. Only the last fight ruined the immersion a little bit.

[h2]Time's Up[/h2]
[b]Remedy makes incredible games, and Quantum Break is one of them. The game is two-in-one. For one price, you will get a nice action-adventure game along with a well-made TV series. Both have a nice story that is connected and can be changed by your decisions in the game, and by exploring locations you can learn more about the lore and find some easter eggs. Also, the combat system is something different thanks to Jack’s special time abilities. So, I can highly recommend the game to you and I will end this review with the text from the legendary meme image with monkeys: [i]Quantum Break 2 when?[/i][/b]
[spoiler]Remember, the past is set, but present and future not.[/spoiler]

It's a game that plays out more like a movie. Both with cutscenes and 20+min live-action segments, with gameplay in all the middle. Choices you make in game change which cutscenes, live-action segments, and various atmosphere elements appear.

The gameplay is rather unique with the various powers you have, all relating to the usage of time, but your main attacks will be with guns. There is something to be desired in a cover-based shooter that doesn't let you take cover effectively, so you will end up doing hit-and-run attacks while reloading and regenerating your powers. There are also platforming and puzzle elements that revolve around time and your manipulation of it, but it's not very complex or hard. It just requires a fair bit of looking for the one thing you have to manipulate to pass the obstacle.

The gunplay is acceptable. You have your standard pistol, SMG, assault rifle, shotgun, and carbine rifle. No sniper rifles and no scopes. Headshots still do bonus damage and you can 2-shot headshot all the fodder enemies with the starting pistol throughout the game, except at extreme range.

But the main part of this game is the story, which revolves around timetravel and has 2 distinct "loops" of the timeline, which you will piece together via the gameplay itself, various optional documents, cutscenes, and the live-action segments. You can skip the live action segments if you wish, but when the story comes to a head, you will be missing out a fair bit of the story.
Hilariously enough, the major choices you make in the game are from the point of view of the antagonist, with short previews of what will happen for each option. Then you switch back to the perspective of the protagonist.

As for replayability, even though there are a few major choices throughout the game, they don't seem to make too much of a difference to the gameplay itself and don't change the overarching story. Replayability immediately after the first playthrough would be tedious due to the spacing left between objectives for the story to be discussed/read to the player.

It's a great game to get on sale!
